title: LLM App Safety and Observability: Injection, Guardrails, Tool Permissions, RAG Evals and Tracing
summary: Quick revision notes on defending LLM apps against prompt injection, layering input and output guardrails, scoping tool permissions, scoring RAG quality with faithfulness and relevance, and tracing every step in production.

chapters.title: Prompt Injection: The Threat Model
points: Prompt injection: untrusted text is read by the model as instructions. LLMs have no hard boundary between instructions and data, so the system prompt and a user or document string sit in one token stream.

Direct injection comes from the user turn ("ignore previous instructions"). Indirect injection hides in content the app fetches (web page, PDF, email, RAG chunk, tool result) and is the more dangerous kind because the user never sees it.

Jailbreak vs injection: a jailbreak makes the model break its own safety policy; an injection hijacks the app's task or tools. Injection is an application-security problem, not only a model-alignment one.

Worst case is the 'lethal trifecta': private data access + exposure to untrusted content + an exfiltration channel (outbound link, image URL, email tool). Remove any one leg and the attack chain breaks.
Interview Point: Why can't you fully fix prompt injection with a better system prompt? How does indirect injection differ from direct, and give one exfiltration route via a markdown image URL.

chapters.title: Input and Output Guardrails
points: Input guardrails run before the model: length limits, PII redaction, injection and jailbreak classifiers, topic allowlists, and stripping or delimiting untrusted content. They reduce risk but never eliminate it.

Output guardrails run after the model: schema validation (JSON or Pydantic), PII and secret scanning, toxicity or policy classifiers, URL and markdown-image allowlists, and groundedness checks. They are the last line before the user or a tool sees the text.

Rules vs model-based checks: regex and schema checks are fast, deterministic and cheap but brittle; LLM or classifier guards generalise but add latency, cost and their own false positives and can themselves be injected.

Pattern: guard in, guard out, fail closed. On a block, return a safe fallback message, log the reason code, and never retry blindly with the same input. Run cheap guards first and expensive ones only if needed, in parallel where possible.
Interview Point: Where do you put guardrails in the request path and why both sides? How do you handle false positives and added latency? Why is a keyword blocklist alone a common mistake?

chapters.title: Tool Permissions and Least Privilege
points: Treat the model as an untrusted caller: authorize every tool call in code, outside the model. A prompt saying 'do not delete' is not a control; a missing permission is.

Least privilege: give each agent an explicit tool allowlist, read-only credentials by default, narrow scopes, short-lived per-user tokens (act on the user's behalf, not a shared admin key), and validate tool arguments against a schema.

Tiered actions: local read tools (search an index, read a file) auto-run; fetch and browse are egress tools that need an outbound domain allowlist; write, send, spend and delete tools need human-in-the-loop confirmation showing the exact arguments. Add rate limits and spend caps per session.

Isolate risk: run code and shell tools in a sandbox with no network or secrets, and do not let content from an untrusted source trigger privileged tools in the same turn (split into a quarantined reader and a privileged actor).
Interview Point: How would you design permissions for an email-summarising agent that can also send mail? Which leg of the lethal trifecta do you cut, and why is an allowlist safer than a denylist?

chapters.title: Evaluating RAG: Faithfulness and Relevance
points: Evaluate retrieval and generation separately. Retrieval metrics: context precision (are retrieved chunks relevant and well ranked), context recall (was everything needed retrieved), plus hit rate, recall@k and MRR against labelled queries.

Faithfulness (groundedness): are the answer's claims supported by the retrieved context? Compute it by splitting the answer into claims and checking each against the context; score is supported claims / total claims. It catches hallucination.

Answer relevance: does the answer address the question asked? A faithful answer can still be irrelevant (a true quote that does not answer). Faithfulness checks answer vs context; relevance checks answer vs question.

Build a golden set of 50-200 real questions with reference answers and source chunks; use an LLM-as-judge (RAGAS, TruLens, DeepEval style) with a rubric, spot-check it against human labels, and run it on every prompt, chunking or model change as a regression gate.

Interview Point: Answer is fluent but wrong; how do you tell if retrieval or generation failed? Define faithfulness vs answer relevance vs context recall, and name a risk of using an LLM as the judge.

chapters.title: Tracing and Observability for LLM Apps
points: A trace is one request end to end; spans are its steps: retrieval, rerank, prompt build, each LLM call, each tool call, guardrail checks. Nested spans show where time, tokens and errors go in agent loops.

Record per span: input and output (redacted), model and version, prompt template version, token counts, latency, cost, tool arguments and results, guardrail verdicts, and a session or user ID to stitch multi-turn conversations.

Instrument with OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions or an LLM platform (Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, Helicone); auto-instrumentation wraps SDK calls, and you add custom spans around retrieval and tools.

Close the loop: sample production traces, attach user feedback and online eval scores (faithfulness, relevance, refusal rate), alert on cost, p95 latency, error and guardrail-block spikes, and turn failing traces into new golden-set cases.
Interview Point: What do you log to debug a bad agent answer after the fact? How do you handle PII in traces, sampling cost, and linking online eval scores back to a specific prompt version?

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Secure and Observable LLM Apps
points: Threat rules: all retrieved or tool text is untrusted data; indirect injection is the main risk; break one leg of the lethal trifecta (private data, untrusted input, exfiltration channel).

Defence stack: input guard (limits, PII, injection classifier) → least-privilege tools with code-level authorization → output guard (schema, secrets, URL allowlist) → fail closed with a safe fallback.

Permissions checklist: tool allowlist, read-only by default, per-user short-lived tokens, schema-validated arguments, human approval for write, send, spend and delete, sandbox for code, rate and spend caps.
RAG eval table: context precision and recall judge retrieval; faithfulness = answer supported by context; answer relevance = answer addresses the question; gate every change on a golden set.
Interview Point: Summarise the full defence-and-measure loop: which controls prevent injection damage, which metrics detect RAG regressions, and which trace fields let you debug production incidents?
